headline: Colonel Natusch Busch seizes power in Bolivia
summary: On 1 November 1979 Colonel Alberto Natusch Busch overthrew Bolivia's interim civilian president, Walter Guevara Arze, only months after elections.
significance: The coup cut short Bolivia's return to civilian rule and met a general strike and bloody street resistance; Natusch gave way within about two weeks. It was one of a run of Bolivian coups that made the country a byword for instability in Washington's view of the Andes.
fbis: The Latin America Daily Report of 1 November 1979 opened its Bolivia section with a run of coup items: the military ousting President Guevara, Colonel Natusch named as leader and new president, and a presidency spokeswoman condemning the coup.

headline: East Germany reopens its border with Czechoslovakia
summary: On 1 November 1989 East Germany lifted the restrictions it had imposed on travel to Czechoslovakia, reopening the route by which thousands of its citizens were reaching the West through Prague.
significance: The exodus through Czechoslovakia drained the GDR of young workers and showed that its leadership could no longer hold its population in. Eight days later the Berlin Wall opened.
fbis: East Berlin's Voice of GDR reported on 1 November that thousands of GDR citizens had travelled to the CSSR that day after the passport and visa suspension was lifted, with more gathering at the West German embassy in Prague.

headline: American hostage David Jacobsen freed in Beirut
summary: On 2 November 1986 Islamic Jihad released David Jacobsen, director of the American University Hospital in Beirut, after some seventeen months in captivity.
significance: Jacobsen's release was a product of the secret US arms sales to Iran. Within days a Lebanese magazine exposed the dealings, opening the Iran-Contra affair.
fbis: The Middle East & South Asia review of 3 November 1986 relayed AFP's report of Islamic Jihad's release statement, which held the US government "entirely responsible" if it failed to pursue a solution to the hostage issue.

headline: Beirut magazine exposes McFarlane's secret trip to Tehran
summary: On 3 November 1986 the Beirut weekly Ash-Shiraa reported that former US National Security Adviser Robert McFarlane had secretly visited Tehran, revealing American arms sales to Iran.
significance: The story broke open the Reagan administration's covert arms-for-hostages dealings with Iran, contradicting its public embargo and its refusal to bargain with hostage-takers. It led within weeks to the discovery that profits had been diverted to the Nicaraguan contras.
fbis: FBIS's regional review reported that Majlis Speaker Hashemi-Rafsanjani, speaking at a Tehran rally on the embassy seizure anniversary, gave details of McFarlane's visit, saying the Americans had arrived in a cargo plane bearing a message from Reagan.

headline: Mercenaries attempt a coup in the Maldives; India intervenes
summary: On 3 November 1988 Sri Lankan Tamil mercenaries attacked Male in an attempt to overthrow President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom. Indian paratroops flown in that night put down the attempt.
significance: India's swift intervention, at Gayoom's request, showed New Delhi acting as the security guarantor of the Indian Ocean region, and Washington and London welcomed it.
fbis: Delhi radio's English service reported on the morning of 3 November that unidentified gunmen had attacked the presidential palace in Male, and that President Gayoom and his ministers were safe.

headline: Students seize the US Embassy in Tehran
summary: On 4 November 1979 Iranian students who followed Ayatollah Khomeini's line overran the US Embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage.
significance: Fifty-two Americans were held for 444 days. The crisis destroyed US-Iranian relations, dominated the last year of the Carter presidency, and the students later published embassy documents, many of them CIA papers reassembled from shreds.
fbis: The Middle East & North Africa Daily Report of 5 November 1979 gathered Iranian reportage under a single heading on the occupation: students occupying the embassy, staff taken hostage, the seizure of documents and the students' own statement.

headline: Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin assassinated
summary: On 4 November 1995 Yitzhak Rabin was shot dead after a peace rally in Tel Aviv by Yigal Amir, an Israeli opponent of the Oslo accords.
significance: The killing of the prime minister who had signed the Oslo agreements struck at the US-brokered peace process, and exposed a failure by the Shin Bet, which was responsible for his protection.
fbis: The Near East & South Asia report of 6 November 1995 carried Palestinian coverage of an emergency meeting of the PA Council of Ministers to discuss the consequences of Rabin's assassination.

headline: Rabbi Meir Kahane assassinated in New York
summary: On 5 November 1990 Meir Kahane, founder of the Jewish Defense League and the Kach movement, was shot dead in a Manhattan hotel by El Sayyid Nosair.
significance: Kahane was an Israeli extremist figure, and his killing in the United States was later linked to the circle around the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.
fbis: Poorly reproduced in the scan, the Near East & South Asia report of 8 November 1990 carried an unattributed commentary from the Baghdad-based Voice of the PLO under the FBIS heading that the Kahane killing was lauded.

headline: Iran's Prime Minister Bazargan resigns
summary: On 6 November 1979, two days after the seizure of the US Embassy, Mehdi Bazargan resigned as prime minister of Iran's provisional government.
significance: Bazargan's fall removed the last moderate leadership willing to deal with Washington and left power with Khomeini's Revolutionary Council, prolonging the hostage crisis.
fbis: The 6 November 1979 Middle East & North Africa report listed Iranian items on Khomeyni accepting Bazargan's resignation and delegating power, with the text of the letter of resignation.

headline: Re-defected KGB officer Yurchenko flies home to Moscow
summary: On 6 November 1985 Vitaliy Yurchenko, the senior KGB officer who had defected to the United States in August, flew back to Moscow, two days after appearing at the Soviet Embassy in Washington to claim the CIA had drugged and abducted him.
significance: Yurchenko's re-defection embarrassed the CIA and left lasting doubt about whether he had been genuine. His debriefings had already exposed Edward Lee Howard and Ronald Pelton.
fbis: The Soviet Union Daily Report of 6 November 1985 carried an IZVESTIYA dispatch from Washington presenting the affair as the kidnapping of a Soviet diplomat by the US special services, under a section FBIS titled 'Act of State Terrorism'.

headline: M-19 guerrillas seize Colombia's Palace of Justice
summary: On 6 November 1985 guerrillas of the M-19 movement stormed the Palace of Justice in Bogota and took the Supreme Court justices hostage. The army's assault over the next day left about a hundred dead, including eleven justices.
significance: The siege and its violent end were among the darkest episodes of Colombia's conflicts, and fed suspicion of links between the guerrillas and the drug cartels then fighting extradition to the United States.
fbis: The Latin America report of 7 November 1985 led its Colombia section with M-19 rebels occupying the Palace of Justice and taking hostages, including an M-19 communique and a spokesman saying the war begins now.

headline: Ben Ali removes Bourguiba in Tunisia
summary: On 7 November 1987 Prime Minister Zine El Abidine Ben Ali had doctors declare President Habib Bourguiba unfit to rule and took power in Tunisia.
significance: The bloodless 'medical coup' ended the rule of Tunisia's founding president. Ben Ali, a former security chief, would rule until 2011.
fbis: FBIS's Near East & South Asia review reported Ben Ali replacing Bourguiba as president and supreme commander after Bourguiba was declared "totally incapable", citing the new leader's statement broadcast by Tunis radio.

headline: Man fires at Gorbachev's parade on Red Square
summary: On 7 November 1990, during the revolution anniversary parade, a Leningrad man fired a shotgun towards the reviewing stand on Red Square where Mikhail Gorbachev stood. He was overpowered and nobody was hit.
significance: The attempt on the Soviet leader's life underlined how far the country's tensions had come into the open in the last year of the USSR.
fbis: TASS in English reported the same day that several shots rang through Red Square during the official anniversary celebrations; FBIS ran it in that day's Soviet Union report.

headline: IRA bomb kills eleven at Enniskillen Remembrance service
summary: On 8 November 1987 an IRA bomb exploded at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Enniskillen, Northern Ireland, killing eleven people.
significance: The attack on civilians at a memorial caused revulsion across Ireland and Britain and damaged the IRA politically.
fbis: TASS's Russian-language international service reported from London on 8 November a powerful explosion at the war memorial in Enniskillen, citing the Press Association on at least ten dead.

headline: Israel confirms it holds the nuclear whistle-blower Mordechai Vanunu
summary: On 9 November 1986 the Israeli government announced that Mordechai Vanunu, a former technician at the Dimona nuclear centre who had given details of Israel's weapons programme to the Sunday Times, was in custody in Israel.
significance: Vanunu had vanished from London weeks earlier; he had been lured to Rome by a Mossad agent and smuggled to Israel. His revelations exposed the scale of Israel's undeclared nuclear arsenal.
fbis: FBIS's 10 November 1986 regional review reported, from IDF radio, the Israeli government secretariat's statement that Vanunu was being held in Israel under a court order, and its answer to rumours that he had been kidnapped.

headline: Gorbachev and Kohl sign a German-Soviet treaty in Bonn
summary: On 9 November 1990, a year to the day after the Berlin Wall opened, Mikhail Gorbachev and Helmut Kohl signed a treaty of good-neighbourliness, partnership and cooperation in Bonn.
significance: The treaty sealed the new relationship between Moscow and a united Germany, which was paying for the withdrawal of Soviet troops from the former GDR.
fbis: The Soviet Union report of 9 November 1990 carried Moscow previews of Gorbachev's first visit to united Germany, at which he was expected to sign a treaty on good-neighbourly relations, partnership and cooperation.

headline: Todor Zhivkov ousted in Bulgaria
summary: On 10 November 1989 the Bulgarian Communist Party removed Todor Zhivkov, its leader since 1954, replacing him with Foreign Minister Petur Mladenov.
significance: Zhivkov had been the longest-serving leader in the Soviet bloc; his fall, the day after the Berlin Wall opened, showed the collapse spreading across Eastern Europe.
fbis: Albanian radio, citing BTA, reported on 11 November that Zhivkov had resigned his highest party and state posts at a Bulgarian Central Committee plenum held the day before.

headline: Bomb destroys Israeli military headquarters in Tyre
summary: On 11 November 1982 a car bomb destroyed the Israeli military government headquarters in Tyre, southern Lebanon, killing scores of Israeli soldiers and border police and Lebanese prisoners.
significance: Later attributed to the forerunners of Hizballah, it was one of the first suicide bombings of the Lebanon war, a tactic used against the US Embassy and Marines in Beirut in 1983.
fbis: FBIS's Middle East review of 12 November 1982 reported, from Jerusalem radio, that an explosion had devastated the Israeli military headquarters in Tyre early on 11 November, killing at least 26.

headline: Moscow announces the death of Leonid Brezhnev
summary: On 11 November 1982 Soviet radio and television announced that Leonid Brezhnev had died the previous morning.
significance: Brezhnev had led the USSR since 1964. His death opened a period of rapid succession: Andropov, then Chernenko, then Gorbachev.
fbis: The East Europe Daily Report of 12 November 1982 listed reaction across the bloc: Bucharest radio announcing Brezhnev's death, Poland paying homage, and Yugoslav condolences.

headline: FMLN launches its offensive on San Salvador
summary: On 11 November 1989 El Salvador's FMLN guerrillas launched their largest offensive of the war, fighting into San Salvador itself.
significance: The offensive showed that neither side could win militarily and that US aid had not defeated the insurgency, pushing both towards the UN-brokered negotiations that ended the war in 1992.
fbis: The Latin America report of 13 November 1989 carried Salvadoran radio accounts of rebel incursions in the capital, including FMLN urban commandos attacking the bodyguards of the Legislative Assembly president.

headline: Former KGB chief Yuriy Andropov becomes Soviet leader
summary: On 12 November 1982 the Central Committee elected Yuriy Andropov General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, two days after Brezhnev's death.
significance: Andropov had headed the KGB for fifteen years. His accession put an intelligence chief at the top of the Soviet system during one of the tensest periods of the Cold War.
fbis: Sofia's Horizont radio broke into its programme on 12 November 1982: it had just received the news from Moscow that the Central Committee had elected Andropov general secretary.

headline: Indonesian troops fire on mourners in Dili
summary: On 12 November 1991 Indonesian troops opened fire on a funeral procession turned independence demonstration at the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili, East Timor, killing many.
significance: Filmed by a foreign journalist, the massacre turned international attention to Indonesia's occupation of East Timor and strained its relations with Washington.
fbis: The East Asia report of 12 November 1991 carried AFP's same-day dispatch from Jakarta that Indonesian soldiers had fired on a crowd of mourners at a cemetery in Dili.

headline: Nevado del Ruiz eruption buries Armero
summary: On 13 November 1985 the Nevado del Ruiz volcano in Colombia erupted, and mudflows buried the town of Armero, killing over twenty thousand people.
significance: It was one of the deadliest volcanic disasters of the century, coming a week after the Palace of Justice siege.
fbis: AFP's Spanish service reported on 14 November that the town of Armero had disappeared under a layer of mud after the volcano erupted, according to the police.

headline: Car bomb at US military training mission in Riyadh
summary: On 13 November 1995 a car bomb exploded outside a US-run training office for the Saudi National Guard in Riyadh, killing five Americans and two Indians.
significance: It was the first major attack on the US military presence in Saudi Arabia, a precursor of the Khobar Towers bombing in 1996.
fbis: The Near East & South Asia report of 13 November 1995 carried AFP's same-day dispatch that an explosion had ripped through the building housing the Saudi American National Guard development mission, causing American casualties.

headline: US and Britain charge two Libyan intelligence officers over Lockerbie
summary: On 14 November 1991 the United States and Britain announced charges against two Libyans, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah, alleged officers of Libyan intelligence, for the bombing of Pan Am flight 103.
significance: The indictments ended speculation that Iran or Syria had been responsible, and led to UN sanctions on Libya when Tripoli refused to hand the men over.
fbis: Tripoli's JANA carried a statement on 15 November from Libya's People's Bureau for Foreign Liaison denying any Libyan involvement in the Lockerbie bombing.

headline: Prince Sihanouk returns to Phnom Penh
summary: On 14 November 1991 Prince Norodom Sihanouk returned to Phnom Penh after nearly thirteen years in exile, under the Paris peace agreements signed the previous month.
significance: His return was the visible start of the UN-supervised settlement that ended Cambodia's war.
fbis: Phnom Penh's SPK news agency reported on 14 November that Prince Norodom Sihanouk had left China for Cambodia early that morning.

headline: Turkish Cypriots declare an independent state
summary: On 15 November 1983 the Turkish Cypriot assembly declared the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus.
significance: Only Turkey recognised it; the declaration hardened the division of Cyprus between two NATO allies' communities.
fbis: Delhi radio reported on 16 November that India deplored the unilateral declaration of independence by the Turkish-occupied part of Cyprus.

headline: Palestine National Council declares a Palestinian state
summary: On 15 November 1988 the Palestine National Council, meeting in Algiers, proclaimed an independent State of Palestine.
significance: The declaration's implicit acceptance of UN resolutions was a step towards the PLO's recognition of Israel, which opened a US dialogue with the PLO that December.
fbis: An FBIS editorial report described Arafat formally proclaiming the "State of Palestine" at the final PNC session, broadcast live by Algiers television early on 15 November.

headline: Six Jesuit priests murdered in San Salvador
summary: On 16 November 1989 soldiers of the Salvadoran army killed six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper and her daughter at the Central American University in San Salvador.
significance: The killings by a US-trained battalion turned the US Congress against military aid to El Salvador and helped force a negotiated end to the war.
fbis: Madrid's EFE agency reported from San Salvador on 16 November that the Jesuit provincial had confirmed the killing of Ignacio Ellacuria, rector of the Central American University, and other priests, gunned down in their residence.

headline: Police beat students in Prague, starting the Velvet Revolution
summary: On 17 November 1989 riot police attacked a student march in Prague. The beating set off the mass protests that brought down Czechoslovakia's communist government within weeks.
significance: The Velvet Revolution completed the collapse of communist rule in Central Europe in the autumn of 1989.
fbis: Czechoslovak television's evening report of 17 November, which FBIS headed 'Antisocialist' Forces Demonstrate, followed the students' procession for International Students Day as it happened.

headline: Terry Waite and Thomas Sutherland freed in Lebanon
summary: On 18 November 1991 Terry Waite, the Archbishop of Canterbury's envoy, and Thomas Sutherland, an American dean at the American University of Beirut, were released after years as hostages in Lebanon.
significance: Waite had been seized in 1987 while negotiating for hostages, and his contacts with Oliver North made him a figure in the Iran-Contra story. The releases were part of a UN-brokered winding up of the Lebanon hostage crisis.
fbis: AFP reported from Beirut on 18 November that Islamic Jihad had announced the release of Terry Waite and Thomas Sutherland; FBIS carried it the same day.

headline: Vukovar falls to the Yugoslav army
summary: On 18 November 1991 the Croatian town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People's Army and Serb forces after a siege of nearly three months.
significance: The destruction of Vukovar and the killing of prisoners afterwards became emblems of the Yugoslav wars.
fbis: Radio Croatia reported on 18 November that the Yugoslav army commander had written to the EC ambassador in Zagreb about security for EC observers in Vukovar.

headline: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Geneva
summary: On 19 November 1985 Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva for the first US-Soviet summit in six years.
significance: The summit produced little on paper but began the personal relationship that led to the INF Treaty and the end of the Cold War.
fbis: The East Europe report of 20 November 1985 carried bloc coverage of the first day of the Geneva summit, including Warsaw radio's review of the morning papers and notes on the agreed news blackout on the talks.

headline: NATO and Warsaw Pact sign the CFE Treaty in Paris
summary: On 19 November 1990 the members of NATO and the Warsaw Pact signed the Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe in Paris.
significance: The treaty imposed deep cuts in tanks, artillery and aircraft, ending the Soviet superiority in Europe that NATO planning had faced for forty years.
fbis: CTK reported on 18 November that President Havel had left for the Paris CSCE meeting, which was to ratify the treaty on conventional armed forces cuts.

headline: Armed militants seize the Grand Mosque in Mecca
summary: On 20 November 1979 several hundred armed militants led by Juhayman al-Otaybi seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca. Saudi forces retook it after two weeks of fighting.
significance: False rumours of US involvement led mobs to attack the US Embassy in Islamabad the next day. The siege pushed the Saudi monarchy towards stricter religious policies.
fbis: The Middle East & North Africa report of 21 November 1979 listed Saudi coverage of the seizure of the Haram mosque: an Interior Ministry statement and Riyadh's assurance that the situation was under control.

headline: Mob burns the US Embassy in Islamabad
summary: On 21 November 1979 a mob, roused by false reports that the United States was behind the seizure of the Grand Mosque in Mecca, stormed and burned the US Embassy in Islamabad. Four people died, two of them Americans.
significance: Coming weeks after the Tehran embassy seizure, it showed the vulnerability of American diplomats across the region.
fbis: The 21 November 1979 report listed AFP's account of the mob attack on the US Embassy in Islamabad, staff taking refuge in the basement, and Karachi radio reporting that demonstrators had set the embassy on fire.

headline: Bosnian peace agreement initialled at Dayton
summary: On 21 November 1995, after three weeks of talks at an Air Force base in Dayton, Ohio, the presidents of Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia initialled a peace agreement.
significance: The Dayton agreement ended the Bosnian war and committed NATO, including US troops, to enforce it.
fbis: The East Europe report of 21 November 1995 carried Bosnian radio items from the last days of the Dayton talks, including Bosnian Muslim party support for the Dayton agreement on the Federation.

headline: Lebanese President Rene Moawad assassinated
summary: On 22 November 1989, seventeen days after taking office under the Taif Agreement, Lebanese President Rene Moawad was killed by a bomb in West Beirut.
significance: His assassination struck at the Arab-brokered settlement meant to end the civil war; Elias Hrawi was elected in his place two days later.
fbis: Beirut's Voice of Lebanon broke the news on 22 November: a booby-trapped car had exploded near the president's motorcade moments after he left Government House, and Mu'awwad was "martyred".

headline: EgyptAir flight 648 hijacked to Malta
summary: On 23 November 1985 Abu Nidal gunmen hijacked an EgyptAir flight from Athens and forced it down in Malta. Egyptian commandos stormed the plane the next day and some sixty people died.
significance: One of the deadliest hijackings of the decade, it came weeks after the Achille Lauro affair and fed US pressure to act against states sponsoring terrorism.
fbis: FBIS's regional review of 26 November 1985 cited TANJUG on a joint communique in which Abu Nidal's faction and an 'Organization of Egypt's Revolutionaries' claimed the hijacking.

headline: Czechoslovak communist leadership resigns
summary: On 24 November 1989, after a week of mass demonstrations, Milos Jakes and the Czechoslovak Communist Party leadership resigned.
significance: The resignation, a week after the student march was beaten, showed how fast the Velvet Revolution had broken the regime.
fbis: Prague's domestic service reported on the night of 24 November that Milos Jakes had spoken at the emergency Central Committee session and that Karel Urbanek had been elected general secretary.

headline: Iran-Contra diversion announced; Poindexter resigns, North fired
summary: On 25 November 1986 Attorney General Edwin Meese announced that proceeds from secret arms sales to Iran had been diverted to the Nicaraguan contras. National Security Adviser John Poindexter resigned and Lt. Col. Oliver North was dismissed.
significance: The diversion turned an embarrassing arms deal into a constitutional scandal over a covert operation run from the White House in defiance of Congress's ban on aid to the contras.
fbis: Havana's Radio Progreso said on 26 November that Reagan's credibility was in a 'spiraling descent', reporting Meese's disclosure that Iran's payments had gone to the contra leaders and that North and Poindexter had been fired.

headline: Hungarians vote in the 'four yeses' referendum
summary: On 26 November 1989 Hungarians voted narrowly to delay the presidential election until after a new parliament was chosen, and to abolish the party's workplace cells and militia.
significance: The result denied the reform communists an early presidential vote they expected to win, opening the way to a fully democratic transition.
fbis: The East Europe report of 27 November 1989 carried Budapest coverage around the referendum, including Hungarian political organisations' views on whether it sharpened domestic tensions.

headline: Medellin cartel bombs Avianca flight 203
summary: On 27 November 1989 a bomb planted by the Medellin cartel destroyed Avianca flight 203 shortly after take-off from Bogota, killing all 107 aboard.
significance: The bombing was part of Pablo Escobar's war against extradition to the United States; two Americans were among the dead, which gave US courts jurisdiction.
fbis: Madrid's EFE reported from Bogota on 27 November that an Avianca Boeing 727 with 107 people aboard had exploded shortly after take-off, with no survivors reported.

headline: Second coup attempt in a year in Venezuela
summary: On 27 November 1992 rebel officers tried for the second time that year to overthrow President Carlos Andres Perez of Venezuela, seizing a television station and bombing Caracas from the air before being defeated.
significance: The failure of both 1992 coups left Perez weakened; he was impeached the following year. The February attempt had been led by Hugo Chavez.
fbis: FBIS's Latin America summary of 27 November 1992 reported international and local media saying a coup led by the 'Revolutionary Bolivarian Movement 200' was under way, with fighting in Caracas.

headline: Kohl presents his ten-point plan for German unity
summary: On 28 November 1989 West German Chancellor Helmut Kohl presented a ten-point programme to the Bundestag for overcoming the division of Germany.
significance: The plan was the first open step towards reunification, and surprised allies and Moscow alike.
fbis: East Berlin's ADN reported on 28 November that Egon Krenz, interviewed on West German television, rejected preconditions for negotiations, under FBIS's heading on reaction to Kohl's 10-point programme.

headline: Margaret Thatcher leaves office; John Major succeeds her
summary: On 28 November 1990 Margaret Thatcher formally resigned as British prime minister and John Major took office.
significance: Thatcher had been Reagan's closest ally in the late Cold War and one of the first Western leaders to embrace Gorbachev.
fbis: The Soviet Union report's contents for early December listed a SOVETSKAYA ROSSIYA article of 29 November assessing John Major as 'Thatcher's man'.

headline: Korean Air flight 858 destroyed by North Korean agents
summary: On 29 November 1987 Korean Air flight 858 exploded over the Andaman Sea, killing all 115 aboard. A bomb had been planted by two North Korean intelligence agents; one, Kim Hyon-hui, survived to confess.
significance: The bombing, aimed at disrupting the 1988 Seoul Olympics, led the United States to put North Korea on its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
fbis: The Near East & South Asia report of 1 December 1987 listed, under Bahrain, a Tokyo KYODO item quoting a Bahraini official on the suspects in the South Korean jet bombing, the two North Korean agents detained there.

headline: Uruguayans reject the military's constitution
summary: On 30 November 1980 voters in Uruguay rejected, in a plebiscite, a draft constitution proposed by the ruling military that would have entrenched the armed forces' role in government.
significance: The defeat was a rare instance of a military regime losing its own referendum, and began Uruguay's slow return to civilian rule in 1985.
fbis: The Latin America report of 1 December 1980 listed Argentine reaction under the heading that Argentines voiced satisfaction at the Uruguayan vote.

headline: US-Soviet talks on intermediate-range missiles open in Geneva
summary: On 30 November 1981 the United States and the Soviet Union opened negotiations in Geneva on intermediate-range nuclear forces in Europe.
significance: The talks followed Reagan's 'zero option' proposal; they broke down in 1983 when Pershing II deployment began, but resumed and produced the INF Treaty in 1987.
fbis: The East Europe report of 30 November 1981 carried bloc commentary backing the Soviet proposal for a moratorium on new intermediate-range missiles during the Geneva negotiations beginning that Monday.
